implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the acquired handle in a holder that exposes the normal interface; wrap the acquisition in a one-time guard so the factory runs at most once and the result is published with the runtime's memory-order guarantees (once flag, lazy value, Lazy<T>, holder class, double-checked publication). Keep acquisition itself in a separate strategy - supplier, factory, initializer - so transport, credential and retry policy change without touching clients, and give the holder an owner that closes or releases the resource at the end of its scope. Model both states explicitly (not yet acquired, acquired) and decide the error semantics (cache the failure or retry it). Never leave the acquisition unguarded in code that can run concurrently, and never defer resources the process must have to be considered healthy.
code_sketch:
holder.get():
    if not initialized:            # guard: at most once, memory-model correct
        value = factory.acquire()  # may fail: decide cache vs retry
        publish(value)             # visible to all threads afterwards
    return value
# owner.close() releases the resource when the scope ends
pitfalls: Unguarded check-then-assign: the classic data race and double acquisition.
No owner: the lazily acquired resource is never released.
Deferring boot-critical resources turns a start-up error into a runtime one, and with caching guards into a permanent one.

Wrong move: hand-write double-checked locking without a memory-model guarantee -> another thread can observe a non-null but partially initialized resource -> instead use the runtime's one-time guard or a correctly synchronized holder.
